title: Structural complexity of an SU(3) Fermi Hubbard model
authors: Jiani Fu, Zewen Zhang, Eduardo Ibarra-García-Padilla
abstract: Two-dimensional quantum gas microscopy provides an unparalleled tool to study quantum many-body systems using ultracold atoms. For the SU(2) Fermi Hubbard model (FHM), access to spin-resolved projective measurements has been vital for quantifying correlation functions and mapping out the phase diagram. Recent progress in quantum gas microscopy for experiments with ultracold alkaline-earth atoms, which are well described by the SU(N) FHM and are predicted to host exotic ground-state phases, calls for the development of theory-free numerical techniques to extract physical information from their projective measurements. To that end, we evaluate the multiscale structural complexity of snapshots of an SU(3) FHM in the square lattice at $1/3$-filling. We employ mean-field theory to generate spin-resolved density distributions and compute their structural complexity using rectangular coarse-graining windows. We demonstrate that these complexities are linked to relevant physical observables such as the entanglement entropy, and are extremely sensitive for locating phase boundaries. The results presented here validate the structural complexity as an efficient and reliable tool for analyzing the outputs of SU(N) quantum gas microscopes, offering a theory-free property, immediately accessible to experiments.
summary: This work introduces structural complexity as a novel, theory-free diagnostic tool for analyzing quantum many-body systems modeled by the SU(3) Fermi Hubbard Model. By applying this measure to mean-field snapshots, the authors demonstrate that structural complexity correlates strongly with entanglement entropy and accurately maps out the complex phase diagram of the system. This validates the technique for interpreting future measurements from quantum gas microscopes.
main_problem: Developing theory-free numerical techniques to extract physical information from spin-resolved projective measurements of quantum many-body systems.
main_result: Structural complexity was shown to be strongly correlated with entanglement entropy and proved to be an efficient, theory-free tool for accurately locating phase boundaries in the SU(3) FHM.
method: The study uses mean-field theory to generate spin-resolved density distributions, followed by calculating structural complexity via rectangular coarse-graining windows.
model_or_system: The system is the SU(3) Fermi Hubbard Model (FHM) studied on a 2D square lattice at 1/3-filling, relevant to ultracold alkaline-earth atoms.
key_observables: Structural Complexity ($C_0, C_1$), Entanglement Entropy ($S_E$), and spin-resolved density distributions ($\langle n_{i\sigma} angle$).
important_parameters: Interaction strength ratio ($U/t$), filling fraction (1/3), and phase boundaries defined by $U/t$ (e.g., 3.50, 4.75, 5.65).
main_assumptions: The primary approximation used is Mean-Field Theory (MFT) to generate the initial density snapshots for analysis.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows mean-field ground state density profiles illustrating transitions between metallic, tooth, zig-zag, and stripe phases. Figure 3 demonstrates the strong proportionality between $C_0$ and $S_E(N/2)$, and the alignment of their derivatives at phase boundaries.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the problem of analyzing SU(N) FHM measurements, then details the structural complexity measure applied to MFT snapshots, and finally presents results showing the correlation between complexity, entanglement entropy, and phase diagram mapping.
why_interesting: It bridges the gap between advanced theoretical diagnostics (structural complexity, entanglement entropy) and direct, theory-free interpretation of cutting-edge experimental data from quantum gas microscopes.

Results for the other two spin flavors (not shown) are related by translations. At U/t = 3.0, ⟨niσ⟩is spatially uniform and consistent with a metallic phase. As the interaction strength increases, the tooth phase is observed (U/t = 4.0), then the zig-zag phase (U/t = 5.5), and finally the stripe phase (U/t = 5.8).
